title: House and Room
premise: Quentin Galloway's late-night radio show has always been a refuge for the lonely — until callers begin phoning in who died the week before, each one asking her to 'let them finish.' When the village of Marrow Fen's church bell rings at midnight despite being melted down in 1911, Quentin discovers the sound is an invitation, and that her grandmother was one of those who answered it a century ago. Trapped in the vicarage through one long night with the villagers she once dismissed, she learns the house itself was built as a mouth, and something beneath the fen has been waiting to be fed a family. To survive until sunrise, Quentin must choose between the duty of silence her bloodline demands and the love of the people the dead are calling home — and the ending hinges on which voice she finally lets on air.
about_author: Kestrel Iversen grew up in a decommissioned signal station on the Norfolk coast, where the family swore the static sometimes spoke. Their fiction blends folk horror with intimate grief, and they still refuse to own a landline.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Quentin hosts her 2 a.m. call-in show, trading warm banter with insomniacs across the county. A caller named Edith describes drowning in the fen last Tuesday; Quentin checks the obituaries and finds her. POV: Quentin. Beat: unease disguised as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Second Caller
chapters.summary: A man phones in asking his wife to forgive him; Quentin recognizes the voice of Tom Verrity, buried three days ago. She cuts the line, tells herself it's a prank. POV: Quentin. Beat: denial hardening into ritual.

chapters.title: Marrow Fen
chapters.summary: Quentin drives to the village to research Edith, passing the roofless church and its empty bell tower. An old woman warns her not to answer anything that calls after dark. POV: Quentin. Beat: dread taking root in ordinary daylight.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Tape
chapters.summary: In her late grandmother's attic, Quentin finds reel-to-reel recordings from 1974: her grandmother interviewing villagers about the bell, cut off mid-sentence by a sound like a struck throat. POV: Quentin. Beat: inheritance revealed as burden.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Parish records confirm the bell was melted for scrap in 1911, yet every generation reports hearing it toll on the anniversary of the melting. Quentin books a room at the vicarage B&B. POV: Quentin. Beat: curiosity outrunning fear.

chapters.title: Check-In
chapters.summary: Vicarage owner Ruth Halloway is welcoming but strange: no mirrors in the guest rooms, salt in the tea caddy, doors that must be closed in order. POV: Quentin. Beat: hospitality with rules underneath.

chapters.title: First Toll
chapters.summary: At midnight the bell rings — felt in the teeth before it's heard. Every villager within earshot stops mid-motion, faces turning toward the tower like compasses. POV: Quentin. Beat: the invitation made audible.

chapters.title: Pulled
chapters.summary: Quentin wakes standing barefoot in the churchyard, mud to her knees, no memory of leaving bed. The tower door stands open onto darkness. POV: Quentin. Beat: loss of bodily sovereignty.

chapters.title: The Congregation
chapters.summary: Villagers gather at dawn, some weeping, some serene. Ruth explains, without apology: when the bell rings, the called must gather, and someone must hold the door till sunrise. POV: Quentin. Beat: community as conspiracy of survival.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Ruth shows Quentin the parish ledger: in 1911 the village sold its bell to buy its safety, but the buyer's contract required a Galloway to keep vigil whenever it rings again. Her family never left. POV: Quentin. Beat: duty inherited without consent.

chapters.title: Edith's Request
chapters.summary: Edith appears at the vicarage window, dripping, polite, asking only to finish the sentence she died saying. Quentin nearly opens the latch. POV: Quentin. Beat: compassion weaponized against her.

chapters.title: Tom on the Line
chapters.summary: Back in her room, the radio switches itself on. Tom Verrity's voice fills the room, begging forgiveness, growing more wrong with each repetition. POV: Quentin. Beat: love distorted into lure.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Ruth teaches the vigil protocol: no answering voices you know, no crossing thresholds uninvited, count the bells, never the ninth. The house groans like a stomach. POV: Quentin. Beat: structure as armor.

chapters.title: The Mouth Beneath
chapters.summary: In the cellar, Quentin finds the foundation stone carved with a yawning face — the vicarage was raised over the old bell pit, and the fen below remembers being hungry. POV: Quentin. Beat: the house itself implicated.

chapters.title: Sunrise, Almost
chapters.summary: The first night passes; the bell falls silent at 5:47. Villagers disperse, changed — quieter, missing small memories. Quentin decides to stay for the second night anyway. POV: Quentin. Beat: false relief.

chapters.title: Missing Hours
chapters.summary: Quentin reviews her own broadcast archive and hears herself, on tape, hosting a show at 3 a.m. she has no memory of doing — her voice reading names from the ledger. POV: Quentin. Beat: self-betrayal discovered.

chapters.title: The Ninth Bell
chapters.summary: Second midnight: eight tolls, then a pause stretched taut. The whole village holds its breath. The ninth never comes — because something is waiting for Quentin to ring it herself. POV: Quentin. Beat: suspense by omission.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth admits the Halloways have been feeding the vigil volunteers' names to the thing for generations, choosing outsiders so the village could survive. Quentin was chosen years ago. POV: Ruth. Beat: ally revealed as architect.

chapters.title: Run or Ring
chapters.summary: Quentin tries to leave; the road loops back to the churchyard no matter the direction. Her car radio plays her grandmother's tapes, now continuing past where they cut off. POV: Quentin. Beat: trap closing.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: At the fen's edge, the dead stand waist-deep in black water, singing harmonies to a bell that isn't there. Among them, a woman with Quentin's face and her grandmother's hands. POV: Quentin. Beat: awe braided with horror.

chapters.title: Blood and Broadcast
chapters.summary: Quentin realizes her show has been the modern vigil — ten years of open lines keeping the thing listening instead of rising. The dead callers were testing whether she'd hand them the microphone. POV: Quentin. Beat: her vocation reframed as sacrifice.

chapters.title: What Edith Wanted
chapters.summary: Quentin lets Edith finish her sentence over the air: a name, her daughter's, spoken so the living girl can finally grieve. The fen recedes an inch. Kindness works — briefly. POV: Quentin. Beat: hope kindled.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Some villagers, led by Ruth's son Daniel, want Quentin to ring the ninth bell and end the century of vigils forever, whatever it costs. Others want her gone before sunrise. POV: Daniel. Beat: community fracturing.

chapters.title: Third Night Falls Early
chapters.summary: Darkness arrives at four in the afternoon. The bell begins tolling out of sequence — two, five, seven — and the house starts rearranging its rooms around Quentin. POV: Quentin. Beat: reality losing its footing.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: Quentin wanders corridors that become 1911: gaslight, mourning clothes, her great-grandmother keeping the same vigil, failing the same way. The past is a corridor she's walking into. POV: Quentin. Beat: history as haunted present.

chapters.title: The Great-Grandmother's Bargain
chapters.summary: In the vision-night, the 1911 Galloway matriarch confesses she invited the thing in — traded the bell's voice for her dying child's breath. The debt has compounded ever since. POV: Great-grandmother Agnes. Beat: origin of the curse.

chapters.title: Daniel's Betrayal
chapters.summary: Daniel locks Quentin in the bell tower with the rope in reach, believing one clean sacrifice beats endless vigils. He weeps while he does it. POV: Daniel. Beat: love twisted into cruelty.

chapters.title: Tower
chapters.summary: Alone above the village, Quentin hears every dead caller at once, patient, gentle, certain she'll pull the rope. She ties the rope off to nothing and speaks to them instead. POV: Quentin. Beat: defiance as character crystallized.

chapters.title: On Air
chapters.summary: Quentin hotwires the transmitter and broadcasts live from the tower, opening the lines to the dead — letting them speak their unfinished sentences to whoever still listens. The tolling falters. POV: Quentin. Beat: climax igniting.

chapters.title: The Names
chapters.summary: One by one the dead say their names and are answered by the living — Edith's daughter on the phone, Tom's widow at the vicarage gate. Each exchange shrinks the hunger below. POV: multiple, braided. Beat: love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Ruth, keeper of the ledger, burns it on the altar steps, voiding the contract her family enforced. The house screams. She does not stop burning. POV: Ruth. Beat: sacrifice of the gatekeeper.

chapters.title: Ninth Bell
chapters.summary: With the contract ash, the ninth toll comes on its own — and Quentin answers it not with the rope but with her voice, ringing the frequency the bell used to carry. The tower shakes apart around the sound. POV: Quentin. Beat: climax peak.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Light hits the fen. The water goes still and merely wet. The dead bow, one by one, and go down like divers, at peace or at least finished. POV: Quentin. Beat: release.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The village counts what remains: Ruth gone, Daniel hollowed, the church tower empty but no longer listening. Quentin broadcasts one final show, signing off the frequency forever. POV: Quentin. Beat: grief with gratitude in it.

chapters.title: What Belongs to Whom
chapters.summary: Quentin sorts her grandmother's tapes, deciding what to keep and what to bury in the bell pit. Belonging, she concludes, is something you choose aloud, not something you inherit in silence. POV: Quentin. Beat: theme resolved.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the studio phone rings once at 2 a.m. Quentin answers. Static, then — faintly — her grandmother's voice saying thank you, and goodbye. POV: Quentin. Beat: bittersweet closure.

chapters.title: New Neighbors
chapters.summary: Marrow Fen takes in new families; Quentin teaches them the old rules anyway, softened into courtesies: close doors kindly, answer your people, count the bells just in case. POV: Daniel. Beat: cautious renewal.

chapters.title: The Empty Tower
chapters.summary: The village votes to leave the tower roofless, a skylight to the sky. Children play there. Nothing rings. Quentin visits and, for the first time, feels the village hold her rather than owe her. POV: Quentin. Beat: belonging earned.

chapters.title: House and Room
chapters.summary: Quentin buys the vicarage, keeps the salt in the tea caddy out of respect rather than fear, and gives every room a mirror. The house settles, a body digesting at last. POV: Quentin. Beat: home reclaimed.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Years on, Quentin trains a successor for a new late-night show, teaching her the real rule: everyone who calls deserves to finish their sentence. The final image is the transmitter light glowing steady over a quiet fen. POV: Quentin. Beat: peace, watched over.
